lead: Arithmetic and logical instructions are the ALU's commands. They add, subtract, multiply, divide, compare, AND, OR, XOR, complement, rotate and adjust decimal results. Each instruction takes operands and computes a result. Most write a result back and update flags; compare instructions only set flags, and INR/DCR and INX/DCX leave carry (or all flags) untouched. The flags remember the last ALU result: zero, sign, carry, auxiliary carry, parity and overflow. Later branch instructions read those flags, so one compare can drive a decision. A calculator, a UPI amount check, or a motor speed limit test all reduce to these instructions plus a branch.
prereq: You need: data movement in 3.3 and the flag register from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Arithmetic instructions compute in the ALU and change flags. On the 8085: ADD adds a byte to A; ADC adds with carry; SUB subtracts; SBB subtracts with borrow; INR/DCR change a byte by one; INX/DCX change a register pair by one; DAD adds a pair to HL; CPI compares A with an immediate byte; CMP compares A with a register or memory byte and leaves A unchanged. On the 8086, MUL/IMUL multiply unsigned/signed; byte results go to AX, word results to DX:AX. DIV/IDIV divide and store quotient and remainder. The 8051 has ADD, ADDC, SUBB, MUL AB, DIV AB and DA A.

Flags record the last ALU result. C is carry out of bit 7, or a borrow in subtraction. AC is carry from bit 3 to bit 4; in subtraction AC = 1 means a borrow from bit 4, just as C = 1 means a borrow from bit 8. S copies bit 7. Z is 1 when all result bits are 0. P is parity: the 8085 uses even parity, the 8051 uses odd. OV is signed overflow: the result does not fit the signed range. The 8085 has no OV flag; the 8086 and 8051 do. INR/DCR do not affect C. INX/DCX affect no flags. DAD affects only C.

Logical instructions work bit by bit. AND clears bits where the mask has 0; use it to test or keep selected bits. OR sets bits where the mask has 1. XOR toggles bits where the mask has 1. CMA on the 8085 and NOT on the 8086 complement every bit. These pack status bits, select an I/O device, or clear a field. RAL and RAR move bits through carry; RLC and RRC rotate A circularly and also copy the bit that falls off into C. RLC rotates A left; bit 7 goes to C and to bit 0. RRC rotates A right; bit 0 goes to C and to bit 7. RAL rotates left through carry; old C enters bit 0 and bit 7 enters C. RAR rotates right through carry; old C enters bit 7 and bit 0 enters C. The 8085 has DAA only; it has no decimal-adjust instruction for subtraction. DAA adjusts A after packed BCD addition. DAS is an 8086 instruction; it adjusts after BCD subtraction. The 8051 uses DA A only after addition. Bit-manipulation instructions are a related group: SETB, CLR and CPL act on one bit in the 8051, while the 8086 has TEST, which ANDs two operands only to set flags; bit test and modify instructions (BT, BTS, BTR, BTC) come with the 386 and later. Use them for flags, port pins and single status bits.

figure.caption: The ALU takes the two operands, writes 1BH back to A, then sets the flags. Carry and overflow answer different questions.

spec.title: How an ALU instruction runs
spec.aria: A four-step flow: fetch operands, run the ALU operation, write the result, then update the flags register.

nodes.label: Update flags
nodes.note: C=1 AC=1 S=0 Z=0 P=1 OV=0

examples.question: 8085: A = 9CH and B = 7FH. Execute ADD B. Find A and the flags C, AC, S, Z and P. Also give the signed-overflow condition OV that an 8086 would report.
steps: ADD B: A ← A + B. Sum = 156 + 127 = 283₁₀ = 11B₁₆. Low byte = 1B₁₆ = 27₁₀. Carry out of bit 7 = 1.
AC: low nibble C₁₆ + F₁₆ = 12 + 15 = 27 > 15, so carry from bit 3 to bit 4 = 1.
P: 1BH = 0001 1011₂ has four 1 bits, an even number, so P = 1.
Signed OV: 9CH = −100, 7FH = +127, sum = +27, which fits −128 to +127, so OV = 0. The 8085 has no OV flag; an 8086 would show OV = 0.
examples.answer: A = 1BH (27 decimal), C = 1, AC = 1, S = 0, Z = 0, P = 1, OV = 0.
examples.check:
a = 0x9C
b = 0x7F
s = a + b
res = s & 0xFF
c = 1 if s > 0xFF else 0
ac = 1 if ((a & 0x0F) + (b & 0x0F)) > 0x0F else 0
sf = 1 if res & 0x80 else 0
zf = 1 if res == 0 else 0
pf = 1 if bin(res).count('1') % 2 == 0 else 0
ov = 1 if ((a ^ res) & (b ^ res) & 0x80) else 0
print(res)
print(c)
print(ac)
print(sf)
print(zf)
print(pf)
print(ov)

traps: Carry and overflow are different: C is unsigned carry or borrow; OV is signed overflow. In subtraction, C = 1 means a borrow, not a negative result.
INR and DCR do not affect C. INX and DCX affect no flags. DAD affects only C.
On the 8085 only DAA exists. On the 8086, DAA follows BCD addition and DAS follows BCD subtraction. The 8051 has DA A and uses it only after addition.
CMP and CPI set flags by subtraction but do not change A. Do not treat them as SUB.

MUL and IMUL put results in fixed registers and set CF/OF; DIV and IDIV store quotient and remainder in fixed registers. DIV and IDIV leave all flags undefined; do not test a flag after them. MUL and IMUL set only CF and OF (with SF, ZF, AF, PF undefined).

quiz.q: Define C, AC, S, Z, P and OV.
quiz.a: C is carry or borrow; AC is carry from bit 3 to bit 4; S copies bit 7; Z is 1 for a zero result; P is parity; OV is signed overflow.

quiz.q: Why do INR and DCR not affect the carry flag on the 8085?
quiz.a: They are byte increment and decrement. Carry is kept for multi-byte add and subtract, so INR and DCR leave C unchanged.

quiz.q: 8085: A = 7AH, B = 25H. Execute ADD B. Find A, C, AC, S, Z and P.
quiz.a: 7AH + 25H = 9FH. A = 9FH. Low nibbles A + 5 = F, so AC = 0. No carry out, so C = 0. Bit 7 of 9FH is 1, so S = 1. Result is not zero, so Z = 0. 9FH has six 1 bits, so even parity gives P = 1.

quiz.q: Why is DAA used only after BCD addition, not after binary addition?
quiz.a: DAA corrects a packed BCD sum. DAA adds 06H if the low nibble is greater than 9 or AC = 1, and adds 60H if the high nibble is greater than 9 or CY = 1 (both can apply, giving 66H). Binary addition has no BCD nibble rule, so DAA would corrupt it.

quiz.q: 8086: AL = FFH, BL = 02H. Execute MUL BL. Find AX and the CF/OF flags.
quiz.a: FFH × 02H = 01FEH. AX = 01FEH. AH is not zero, so CF = 1 and OF = 1.
RLC rotates A left; bit 7 goes to C and to bit 0. RAL rotates left through carry; old C enters bit 0 and bit 7 enters C.

quiz.q: A student says C = 1 after SUB means the result is negative. Is this correct?
quiz.a: No. C = 1 means a borrow in unsigned subtraction. Sign comes from S, bit 7 of the result. For example, 05H − 07H gives FEH with C = 1 and S = 1.

quiz.q: 8051: A = F6H, R0 = 0AH. Execute ADD A,R0. Find A, C, AC and OV.
quiz.a: F6H + 0AH = 100H. A = 00H. Carry out C = 1. Low nibbles 6 + A = 16 > 15, so AC = 1. Signed −10 + 10 = 0, so OV = 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern CPUs add SIMD integer units that apply one arithmetic or logical operation to many bytes at once. Graphics, audio and cryptography use bit rotates, XOR masks and saturating arithmetic heavily. DSP chips often saturate instead of wrapping on overflow. Search for bit-manipulation instruction sets, BCD arithmetic, SIMD integer arithmetic and saturating arithmetic.
